newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian markets end mostly lower, but Tokyo rises.
newsitem.headline: Asian markets end mostly lower, but Tokyo rises.

text.p: Tokyo's stock market snapped a five-day losing streak on Monday, bucking the bearishness that dragged most other Asian stock exchanges lower.

Tokyo's 225-issue Nikkei average gained 145.44 points, or 0.70 percent, to close at 20,885.41, but brokers warned that turnover was extremely thin as most investors stayed on the sidelines, searching for sound reasons to trade on.
"Trade was extremely dull today and the benchmark Nikkei's rise was feeble and not really strong enough to be considered a rebound," a broker at a second-tier brokerage said.

Brokers said the rise was mainly a reflex reaction to a loss of more than 870 points last week. Investors were quietly awaiting for a new government to emerge following the elections of October 20, they said.
Elsewhere in Asia, the bears ruled.
Hong Kong stocks ended sharply lower, hit by an afternoon slide as a pause in the market's recent rally prompted investors to take profits, brokers said.
The Hang Seng closed 125.61 points, or 1.01 percent, lower at 12,262.77.
"It (the Hang Seng) will probably stabilise around 12,200 and then we will wait for fresh external factors," said Glenn Lesko, head of sales trading at HG Asia.
The Philippine Stock Exchange index took the biggest hit on Monday, suffering its biggest-ever single-day drop. The index plummeted 3.73 percent to close 110 points lower at 2,852.
Investors were spooked by lower-than-expected earnings from blue-chip companies. Monday's slump below the key 2,900 support level has convinced many analysts the gloom would persist.
"We suspect another down move tomorrow as people are still jittery and are rethinking their positions," said Joel Santillan, chief analyst at Asian Oceanic Merit Securities.
Thai stocks dropped for the third consecutive trading day as investors stayed on the sidelines awaiting key economic indicators to be released later this week, brokers said.
The SET index moved in negative territory throughout the day, closing 6.79 points, or 0.72 percent, lower at 931.51 on thin turnover.
"Investors are waiting for economic indicators. They're also concerned about political stability ahead of the November election," said Somnuk Chanrasamee of Nava Finance and Securities.
Seoul shares lost ground nearly across the board in the afternoon session as investors stuck to the sidelines on fears of an oversupply of shares next month, brokers said.
The composite index fell 11.73 points, or 1.48 percent, to a provisional close of 780.08.

"Investors are worried because next month there is expected to be 1.2 trillion won in additional supply to the market, 450 billion won from IPOs," said Kevin Choi, a fund manager at Seoul Investment Trust Co.
Australian shares closed slightly weaker after a bout of selling in the resources sector in the last hour of trading.
The key share-market barometer, the All Ordinaries index, fell 1.1 points, or 0.05 percent, to close at 2,334.1, well off its intra-day high of 2,346.9.

In foreign exchange markets, the dollar powered to a 42-month high against the yen in Tokyo, bolstered by aggressive sales of yen against major currencies. At 1115 GMT, the dollar was trading at 114.20/25 yen and 1.5235/40 marks.
Bullion ended at US$383.00/383.50 an ounce in Hong Kong, against New York's Friday close of US$382.55/383.05.
In Singapore, North Sea Brent December crude oil futures gave up most early gains but still managed to end one cent higher at $24.23 per barrel.
